title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 133 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 622–628 (Night 133, continuing directly from nights-132), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 133 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. The old woman who has come up to Tāj al-Mulūk's shop is the Lady Dunyā's nurse; taken with the young man, she buys cloth for her mistress and carries his praises to the palace. Dunyā laughs, then offers him any favour he needs; he answers with a love letter in verse and rhymed prose. Dunyā is outraged at a merchant writing to a king's daughter, and on the nurse's advice writes back threatening to crucify him; he replies in verse that death would be a rest, and the old woman promises to bring him to his goal. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third and the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirty-third night,
sentences.n: The print spells thalāthūn without its long alif (والثلثون); the small alif over the lām is ours, to show the long vowel.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-ḍawʾi al-makāni
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān went on, telling Ḍawʾ al-Makān:
sentences.n: A reminder of the frame: all of this is the story Dandān is telling King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, inside the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ جَالِسٌ وَإِذَا بِعَجُوزٍ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَتَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَخَلْفَهَا جَارِيَتَانِ وَمَا زَالَتْ مَاشِيَةً حَتَّى وَقَفَتْ عَلَى دُكَّانِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā tāju al-mulūki jālisun wa-idhā bi-ʿajūzin aqbalat ʿalayhi wa-taqaddamat ilayhi wa-khalfahā jāriyatāni wa-mā zālat māshiyatan ḥattā waqafat ʿalā dukkāni tāji al-mulūki
sentences.l: And while Tāj al-Mulūk (was) sitting, behold, an old woman came toward him and advanced to him, and behind her two slave-girls; and she did not cease walking until she stopped at the shop of Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.i: While Tāj al-Mulūk sat there, an old woman came toward him, two slave-girls behind her, and walked on until she stopped at his shop.
sentences.n: The night picks up the last sentence of the night before and tells it again. wa-idhā bi-ʿajūzin, “and behold, an old woman”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears.

sentences.t: فَرَأَتْ قَدَّهُ وَاعْتِدَالَهُ وَحُسْنَهُ وَجَمَالَهُ فَتَعَجَّبَتْ مِنْ مَلَاحَتِهِ وَرَشَحَتْ فِي سَرَاوِيلِهَا ثُمَّ قَالَتْ سُبْحَانَ مَنْ خَلَقَكَ مِنْ مَاءٍ مَهِينٍ وَجَعَلَكَ فِتْنَةً لِلنَّاظِرِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾat qaddahu wa-iʿtidālahu wa-ḥusnahu wa-jamālahu fa-taʿajjabat min malāḥatihi wa-rashaḥat fī sarāwīlihā thumma qālat subḥāna man khalaqaka min māʾin mahīnin wa-jaʿalaka fitnatan li-al-nāẓirīna
sentences.l: And she saw his stature and his straightness and his beauty and his comeliness, and she marvelled at his handsomeness, and she sweated in her trousers; then she said: Glory (be to) who created you from a water despised and made you a temptation for the lookers!
sentences.i: She saw his height and fine proportion, his beauty and his grace, and marvelled at how handsome he was, and grew damp in her drawers. Then she said, “Glory to Him who created you from a despised drop of water and made you a temptation to all who look on you!”
sentences.n: rashaḥat fī sarāwīlihā, “she sweated (or oozed) in her trousers”: a frank, comic sign of the old woman's arousal. min māʾin mahīn, “from a despised water”, is Qurʾānic (77:20), the drop of semen from which man is made; the print marks the mīm of mahīn with its own fatḥa. The rhyme of qaddahu wa-iʿtidālahu / ḥusnahu wa-jamālahu is a stock pair of the Nights.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَأَمَّلَتْ وَقَالَتْ مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا اِنْ هَذَا إِلَّامَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ
sentences.tr: thumma taʾammalat wa-qālat mā hādhā basharan in hādhā illā malakun karīmun
sentences.l: Then she gazed and said: Not this (is) a human; this is not but an angel noble!
sentences.i: Then she looked him over and said, “This is no mortal; this is none other than a noble angel!”
sentences.n: She quotes the Qurʾān (12:31), the words of the women of Egypt on first seeing Joseph. in … illā, “not … but”, with in as a negative. The print runs illā malak together (الاملك), and marks the in with its own kasra (اِنْ).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَنَتْ مِنْهُ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامَ وَقَامَ لَهَا وَاقِفًا عَلَى الْأَقْدَامِ وَتَبَسَّمَ فِي وَجْهِهَا هَذَا كُلُّهُ بِإِشَارَةِ عَزِيزٍ
sentences.tr: thumma danat minhu wa-sallamat ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhā al-salāma wa-qāma lahā wāqifan ʿalā al-aqdāmi wa-tabassama fī wajhihā hādhā kulluhu bi-ishārati ʿazīzin
sentences.l: Then she drew near to him and greeted him, and he returned to her the greeting, and stood for her, standing on the feet, and smiled in her face — this all by the signal of ʿAzīz.
sentences.i: Then she came close and greeted him; he returned her greeting, rose to his feet for her and smiled in her face — all of it at a sign from ʿAzīz.
sentences.n: bi-ishārati ʿazīz, “by ʿAzīz's signal”: bi- of means. ʿAzīz, who has been through all this himself, is coaching the prince by gestures.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَجْلَسَهَا إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَصَارَ يُرَوِّحُ عَلَيْهَا بِمِرْوَحَةٍ حَتَّي اسْتَفَاقَتْ وَاسْتَرَاحَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma ajlasahā ilā jānibihi wa-ṣāra yurawwiḥu ʿalayhā bi-mirwaḥatin ḥattā istafāqat wa-istarāḥat
sentences.l: Then he seated her at his side and began fanning over her with a fan until she came-to and rested.
sentences.i: Then he seated her beside him and fanned her until she had come to herself and rested.
sentences.n: ṣāra yafʿalu, “he began to do”. The print spells ḥattā with a dotted yāʾ (حتي).

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَتِ الْعَجُوزُ إِلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي يَا كَامِلَ الْأَوْصَافِ وَالْمَعَانِي هَلْ أَنْتَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الدِّيَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafatati al-ʿajūzu ilā tāji al-mulūki wa-qālat lahu yā waladī yā kāmila al-awṣāfi wa-al-maʿānī hal anta min hādhihi al-diyāri
sentences.l: And the old woman turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and said to him: O my son, O perfect of the qualities and the meanings, are you from these lands?
sentences.i: Then the old woman turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and said, “My son, perfect in every grace of body and mind, are you from these parts?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ بِكَلَامٍ فَصِيحٍ عَذْبٍ مَلِيحٍ وَاللَّهِ يَا سَيِّدَتِي عُمْرِي مَا دَخَلْتُ هَذِهِ الدِّيَارَ إِلَّا هَذِهِ الْمَرَّةَ وَلَا أَقَمْتُ فِيهَا إِلَّا عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْفُرْجَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā tāju al-mulūki bi-kalāmin faṣīḥin ʿadhbin malīḥin wa-allāhi yā sayyidatī ʿumrī mā dakhaltu hādhihi al-diyāra illā hādhihi al-marrata wa-lā aqamtu fīhā illā ʿalā sabīli al-furjati
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to her, with speech eloquent, sweet, pleasing: By God, O my lady, my life-long I did not enter these lands except this time, and I did not stay in them except by way of the sightseeing.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk answered her in fine, sweet, graceful words, “By God, my lady, never in my life have I come to these parts before this time, and I am staying here only to see the sights.”
sentences.n: ʿumrī mā, “my life (long) not”: colloquial for “never in my life”. al-furja, “sightseeing, a spectacle to enjoy”, a Middle Arabic favourite. bi-kalāmin, “with speech”: bi- of manner.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ أَكْرِمْ بِكَ مِنْ قَادِمٍ عَلَى الرَّحْبِ وَالسَّعَةِ وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ جِئْتَ بِهِ مَعَكَ مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ أَرِنِي شَيْأً مَلِيحًا فَإِنَّ الْمَلِيحَ لَا يَحْمِلُ إِلَّا الْمَلِيحَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat akrim bika min qādimin ʿalā al-raḥbi wa-al-saʿati wa-ayyu shayʾin jiʾta bihi maʿaka mina al-qumāshi arinī shayʾan malīḥan fa-inna al-malīḥa lā yaḥmilu illā al-malīḥa
sentences.l: And she said: How noble you (are) as an arriver! Upon the spaciousness and the roominess! And what thing did you come with, with you, of the cloth? Show me a thing pretty, for the pretty (one) does not carry except the pretty.
sentences.i: She said, “What a noble newcomer you are! Welcome, and room enough! And what cloth have you brought with you? Show me something pretty, for a pretty man carries nothing but pretty things.”
sentences.n: akrim bika, “how noble you are!”: the exclamative form afʿil bi-, where bi- marks the one admired. ʿalā al-raḥbi wa-al-saʿa, “on spaciousness and ampleness”, a welcome. jiʾta bihi, “you brought”: jāʾa bi- means “to bring”. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ كَلَامَهَا خَفَقَ فُؤَادُهُ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ مَعْنَى كَلَامِهَا فَغَمَزَةُ عَزِيزٌ بِالْإِشَارَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa tāju al-mulūki kalāmahā khafaqa fuʾāduhu wa-lam yaʿlam maʿnā kalāmihā fa-ghamazahu ʿazīzun bi-al-ishārati
sentences.l: And when Tāj al-Mulūk heard her speech, his heart fluttered, and he did not know the meaning of her speech; so ʿAzīz winked-at-him with the signal.
sentences.i: When Tāj al-Mulūk heard her, his heart beat fast, and he did not know what she meant; so ʿAzīz gave him a wink and a sign.
sentences.n: The print writes the pronoun -hu of ghamazahu, “he winked at him”, with a final tāʾ marbūṭa (فغمزة), a habit of this edition; read -hu.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عِنْدِي كُلُّمَا تَشْتَهِينَ وَعِنْدِي شَيْءٌ لَايَصْلُحُ إِلَّا لِلْمُلُوكِ وَبَنَاتِ الْمُلُوكِ فَأَخْبِرِينِي بِالشَّيْءِ الَّذِي تُرِيدِينَهُ لِمَنْ حَتَّى أُقَلِّبَ عَلَيْكِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ يَصْلُحُ لِأَرْبَابِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā tāju al-mulūki ʿindī kullu mā tashtahīna wa-ʿindī shayʾun lā yaṣluḥu illā li-al-mulūki wa-banāti al-mulūki fa-akhbirīnī bi-al-shayʾi alladhī turīdīnahu li-man ḥattā uqalliba ʿalayki kulla shayʾin yaṣluḥu li-arbābihi
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to her: With me (is) all-that you desire, and with me (is) a thing (that) is not fit except for the kings and the daughters of the kings; so inform me of the thing which you want — for whom? — so that I turn over before you every thing (that) is fit for its owners.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to her, “I have everything you could wish for, and I have things fit only for kings and kings' daughters. So tell me what you want, and for whom, so that I can turn over for you everything that suits the person it is meant for.”
sentences.n: kullu mā, “all that”, is run together in the print (كلما). li-man, “for whom?”, is set off by the print's own vowels (لِمَنْ). arbāb, “owners, masters”: here the people the goods are for. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: the verb takes bi-.

sentences.t: وَأَرَادَ بِذَلِكَ الْكَلَامِ أَنْ يَفْهَمَ مَعْنَى كَلَامِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-arāda bi-dhālika al-kalāmi an yafhama maʿnā kalāmihā
sentences.l: And he wanted by that speech that he understand the meaning of her speech.
sentences.i: By saying this he meant to find out what she was driving at.
sentences.n: arāda bi-, “to mean by, to intend by”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أُرِيدُ قُمَاشًا يَصْلُحُ لِلسِّتِّ دُنْيَا بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu urīdu qumāshan yaṣluḥu li-al-sitti dunyā binti al-maliki shahramāna
sentences.l: And she said to him: I want cloth (that) is fit for the Lady Dunyā, daughter of the King Shahramān.
sentences.i: She said to him, “I want cloth fit for the Lady Dunyā, daughter of King Shahramān.”
sentences.n: al-sitt, “the lady”, colloquial for sayyida.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ ذِكْرَ مَحْبُوبَتِهِ فَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ لِعَزِيزٍ ائْتِنِي بِالْبُقْجَةِ الْفُلَانِيَّةِ فَأَتَى بِهَا عَزِيزٌ وَحَلَّهَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa tāju al-mulūki dhikra maḥbūbatihi fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan wa-qāla li-ʿazīzin iʾtinī bi-al-buqjati al-fulāniyyati fa-atā bihā ʿazīzun wa-ḥallahā bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And when Tāj al-Mulūk heard the mention of his beloved, he rejoiced a rejoicing strong, and said to ʿAzīz: Bring me the bundle such-and-such. So ʿAzīz brought it and untied it between his hands.
sentences.i: When Tāj al-Mulūk heard his beloved named, he was overjoyed, and said to ʿAzīz, “Bring me such-and-such a bundle.” ʿAzīz brought it and untied it in front of him.
sentences.n: iʾtinī bi-, “bring me”: atā bi-, “to come with”, is “to bring”. buqja, “a cloth bundle” (from Turkish bohça). al-fulāniyya, “such-and-such”: the narrator does not trouble to name which one.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ انْتَخِبِي مَايَصْلُحُ لَهَا فَإِنَّ هَذَا شَيْءٌ لَايُوجَدُ عِنْدَ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā tāju al-mulūki intakhibī mā yaṣluḥu lahā fa-inna hādhā shayʾun lā yūjadu ʿinda ghayrī
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to her: Choose what is fit for her, for this is a thing (that) is not found with other-than-me.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to her, “Choose what suits her; this is something you will find with no one else.”

sentences.t: فَاخْتَارَتِ الْعَجُوزُ شَيْأً يُسَاوِي أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ وَقَالَتْ بِكَمْ هَذَا وَصَارَتِ الْعَجُوزُ تُحَدِّثُهُ وَتَحُكُّ بَيْنَ أَفْخَاذِهَا بِكِلْوَةِ يَدِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ikhtārati al-ʿajūzu shayʾan yusāwī alfa dīnārin wa-qālat bi-kam hādhā wa-ṣārati al-ʿajūzu tuḥaddithuhu wa-taḥukku bayna afkhādhihā bi-kilwati yadihā
sentences.l: And the old woman chose a thing (that) was worth a thousand dinars, and said: For how much (is) this? And the old woman began talking to him and scratching between her thighs with the kidney of her hand.
sentences.i: The old woman picked out a piece worth a thousand dinars and said, “How much is this?” And as she talked with him she kept rubbing between her thighs with the heel of her hand.
sentences.n: bi-kam, “for how much?”: bi- of price. kilwat yadihā, literally “the kidney of her hand”, apparently the fleshy pad at the base of the palm; the expression is unusual and the sense is our best reading.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ وَهَلْ أَنَا أُسَاوِمُ مِثْلَكِ فِي هَذَا الثَّمَنِ الْحَقِيرِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي عَرَّفَنِي بِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā tāju al-mulūki wa-hal anā usāwimu mithlaki fī hādhā al-thamani al-ḥaqīri al-ḥamdu li-allāhi alladhī ʿarrafanī biki
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to her: And do I haggle (with one) like you over this price paltry? The praise (be) to God who acquainted me with you!
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to her, “Would I haggle with someone like you over a trifling price like this? Praise God, who has brought me to know you!”
sentences.n: ʿarrafahu bi-, “to make someone acquainted with”: bi- marks the one he comes to know.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعَجُوزُ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ أُعَوِّذُ وَجْهَكَ الْمَلِيحَ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ الْوَجْهُ مَلِيحٌ وَاللَّفْظُ فَصِيحٌ هَنِيأً لِمَنْ تَنَامُ فِي حِضْنِكَ وَتَضُمُّ قَدَّكَ وَتَحْظَى بِشَبَابِكَ وَخُصُوصًا إِذَا كَانَتْ صَاحِبَةَ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ مِثْلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ʿajūzu ismu allāhi ʿalayka uʿawwidhu wajhaka al-malīḥa bi-rabbi al-falaqi al-wajhu malīḥun wa-al-lafẓu faṣīḥun hanīʾan li-man tanāmu fī ḥiḍnika wa-taḍummu qaddaka wa-taḥẓā bi-shabābika wa-khuṣūṣan idhā kānat ṣāḥibata ḥusnin wa-jamālin mithlaka
sentences.l: And the old woman said to him: The name of God (be) upon you! I seek-refuge for your pretty face in the Lord of the Daybreak! The face (is) pretty and the speech (is) eloquent. Good health to (her) who sleeps in your bosom and clasps your stature and enjoys your youth — and especially if she is an owner of beauty and comeliness like you!
sentences.i: The old woman said to him, “God's name be upon you! I commend your lovely face to the protection of the Lord of the Daybreak! A lovely face and an eloquent tongue! Happy the woman who sleeps in your arms, holds that slender body close and enjoys your youth — above all if she is as beautiful as you!”
sentences.n: The print has وحضوصا, a misprint for wa-khuṣūṣan (وخصوصا), “and especially”, corrected here. ismu allāhi ʿalayka, “God's name upon you”, is said against the evil eye; uʿawwidhu … bi-rabbi al-falaq, “I put (your face) under the protection of the Lord of the Daybreak”, echoes the opening of Qurʾān 113, recited for the same purpose; bi- marks the protector. hanīʾan li-, “may it do good to, happy is”; the print spells it هنيأ. ḥaẓiya bi-, “to enjoy, to win”.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ حَتَّى انْقَلَبَ عَلَى قَفَاهُ ثُمَّ قَالَ يَا قَاضِيَ الْحَاجَاتِ عَلَى أَيْدِى الْعَجَائِزِ الْفَاجِرَاتِ هُنَّ قَاضِيَاتُ الْحَاجَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika tāju al-mulūki ḥattā inqalaba ʿalā qafāhu thumma qāla yā qāḍiya al-ḥājāti ʿalā aydī al-ʿajāʾizi al-fājirāti hunna qāḍiyātu al-ḥājāti
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk laughed until he turned over on his nape; then he said: O Fulfiller of the needs at the hands of the old-women the wanton — they (are) the fulfillers of the needs!
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk laughed until he fell over on his back, and then he said, “O You who fulfil men's needs by the hands of shameless old women — they are the ones who get things done!”
sentences.n: qāḍī al-ḥājāt, “the fulfiller of needs”, is an epithet of God; the prince's joke turns it on the old woman's kind. The sentence is loose, and it may also be read as a proverb: “the fulfiller of needs works through wanton old women; they are the ones who fulfil them.” The print spells aydī with a final ى (ايدى).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي مَااسْمُكَ فَقَالَ اسْمِي تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahu yā waladī mā ismuka fa-qāla ismī tāju al-mulūki
sentences.l: Then she said to him: O my son, what (is) your name? And he said: My name (is) Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.i: Then she asked him, “My son, what is your name?” He said, “My name is Tāj al-Mulūk.”
sentences.n: The print runs mā ismuka together (مااسمك).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُإِنَّ هَذَا اسْمُ الْمُلُوكِ وَأَوْلَادِ الْمُلُوكِ وَأَنْتَ فِي زِيِّ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu inna hādhā ismu al-mulūki wa-awlādi al-mulūki wa-anta fī ziyyi al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And the old woman said: Indeed this (is) a name of the kings and the sons of the kings, and you (are) in the dress of the merchants!
sentences.i: The old woman said, “That is a name for kings and the sons of kings, and you are dressed as a merchant!”
sentences.n: The print runs al-ʿajūzu inna together (العجوزان). Tāj al-Mulūk means “Crown of Kings”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا عَزِيزٌ مِنْ مَحَبَّتِهِ عِنْدَ وَالِدَيْهِ وَأَهْلِهِ وَمَعَزَّتِهِ عَلَيْهِمْ سَمَّوْهُ بِهَذَا الِاسْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ʿazīzun min maḥabbatihi ʿinda wālidayhi wa-ahlihi wa-maʿazzatihi ʿalayhim sammawhu bi-hādhā al-ismi
sentences.l: And ʿAzīz said to her: From his love with his parents and his family, and his dearness upon them, they named him with this name.
sentences.i: ʿAzīz told her, “His parents and family loved him so, and he was so dear to them, that they gave him this name.”
sentences.n: sammāhu bi-, “to name someone (with) a name”. maʿazza, “dearness, esteem”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُ صَدَقْتَ كَفَاكُمُ اللَّهُ شَرَّ الْعَيْنِ وَشَرَّ الْأَعَادِي وَالْحُسَّادِ وَلَوْفَّتَتْ بِمَحَاسِنِكُمُ الْأَكْبَادُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu ṣadaqta kafākumu allāhu sharra al-ʿayni wa-sharra al-aʿādī wa-al-ḥussādi wa-law fattat bi-maḥāsinikumu al-akbādu
sentences.l: And the old woman said: You have spoken-truly. May God suffice you the evil of the eye and the evil of the enemies and the envious — even if the livers crumbled by your beauties.
sentences.i: The old woman said, “You are right. God keep you from the evil eye, and from the malice of enemies and the envious, even though hearts be broken by your beauty!”
sentences.n: kafāhu sharra, “to spare someone the harm of”. The last clause is doubtful. The print reads ولوفّتت, run together, with its doubling mark over the fāʾ; we take it as wa-law fattat(at) (ولو فتّتت), “even if livers crumbled”, with the mark meant for the tāʾ and perhaps a tāʾ lost, and keep the print's letters and mark. The liver, like the heart, is the seat of passion, and to crumble it is to break with love.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَتِ الْقُمَاشَ وَمَضَتْ وَهِيَ بَاهِتَةٌ فِي حُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ وَقَدِّهِ وَاعْتِدَالِهِ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ مَاشِيَةً حَتَّى دَخَلَتْ عَلَى السِّتِّ دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhati al-qumāsha wa-maḍat wa-hiya bāhitatun fī ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi wa-qaddihi wa-iʿtidālihi wa-lam tazal māshiyatan ḥattā dakhalat ʿalā al-sitti dunyā
sentences.l: Then she took the cloth and went, and she (was) dazed in his beauty and his comeliness and his stature and his straightness; and she did not cease walking until she entered upon the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.i: Then she took the cloth and went away, quite dazed by his beauty and grace, his height and fine proportion, and walked on until she came in to the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”, to enter a person's presence.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي جِئْتُ لَكِ بِقُمَاشٍ مَلِيحٍ فَقَالَتْ لَهَا أَرِنِي إِيَّاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahā yā sayyidatī jiʾtu laki bi-qumāshin malīḥin fa-qālat lahā arinī iyyāhu
sentences.l: And she said to her: O my lady, I have come to you with cloth pretty. And she said to her: Show me it.
sentences.i: “My lady,” she said, “I have brought you some lovely cloth.” “Show it to me,” said Dunyā.
sentences.n: jiʾtu bi-, “I have brought”. arinī, “show me”, is the masculine form, used here to a woman; Classical would have arīnī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدَتِي هَاهُوَ فَقَلِّبِيهِ يَاعَيْنِي وَأَبْصِرِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā sayyidatī hā huwa fa-qallibīhi yā ʿaynī wa-abṣirīhi
sentences.l: And she said: O my lady, here it (is); so turn it over, O my eye, and look at it.
sentences.i: She said, “Here it is, my lady; turn it over, my darling, and look at it.”
sentences.n: yā ʿaynī, “O my eye”, an endearment. The print runs yā sayyidatī, hā huwa and yā ʿaynī together.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ السِّتُّ دُنْيَا بَهِتَتْ فِيهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَادَادَتِي إِنَّ هَذَا قُمَاشٌ مَلِيحٌ مَارَأَيْتُهُ فِي مَدِينَتِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu al-sittu dunyā bahitat fīhi wa-qālat lahā yā dādatī inna hādhā qumāshun malīḥun mā raʾaytuhu fī madīnatinā
sentences.l: And when the Lady Dunyā saw it, she was dazed at it, and said to her: O my nurse, indeed this (is) cloth pretty; I have not seen it in our city.
sentences.i: When the Lady Dunyā saw it she was astonished, and said to her, “Nanny, this is lovely cloth; I have never seen its like in our city.”
sentences.n: dāda, “nurse, nanny”, the woman who brought her up. The print sets a doubling mark on al-sitt (الستّ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُ يَاسِتِّي إِنَّ بَائِعَهُ أَحْسَنُ مِنْهُ كَأَنَّ رِضْوَانًا فَتَحَ أَبْوَابَ الْجِنَانِ وَسَهَا فَخَرَجَ مِنْهَا شَابٌّ هُوَ الَّذِي يَبِيعُ هَذَا الْقُمَاشَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu yā sittī inna bāʾiʿahu aḥsanu minhu ka-anna riḍwānan fataḥa abwāba al-jināni wa-sahā fa-kharaja minhā shābbun huwa alladhī yabīʿu hādhā al-qumāsha
sentences.l: And the old woman said: O my lady, indeed its seller (is) more beautiful than it. As if Riḍwān opened the gates of the gardens and was heedless, and there went out from them a youth — he (is) the one who sells this cloth.
sentences.i: The old woman said, “My lady, the man who sells it is lovelier than the cloth. It is as if Riḍwān had opened the gates of Paradise and looked away for a moment, and a youth slipped out — and he is the one selling this cloth.”
sentences.n: Riḍwān is the angel who keeps the gates of Paradise (al-jinān, “the Gardens”). sahā, “to be inattentive, to forget”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَشْتَهِي فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ أَنَّهُ يَنَامُ عِنْدَكِ وَيَكُونُ بَيْنَ نُهُودِكِ فَإِنَّهُ أَتَى مَدِينَتَكِ بِأَقْمِشَةٍ مُثَمَّنَةٍ لِأَجْلِ الْفُرْجَةِ وَهُوَ فِتْنَةٌ لِمَنْ يَرَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-anā ashtahī fī hādhihi al-laylati annahu yanāmu ʿindaki wa-yakūnu bayna nuhūdiki fa-innahu atā madīnataki bi-aqmishatin muthammanatin li-ajli al-furjati wa-huwa fitnatun li-man yarāhu
sentences.l: And I desire in this night that he sleep with you and be between your breasts; for he has come to your city with cloths precious for the sake of the sightseeing, and he (is) a temptation to whoever sees him.
sentences.i: And what I'd like is for him to sleep with you tonight and lie between your breasts. He has come to your city with precious stuffs to see the sights, and he is a temptation to anyone who sees him.”
sentences.n: annahu yanāmu, “that he sleeps”: Middle Arabic puts anna with an ordinary verb where Classical has an yanāma. atā bi-, “to bring”: “he came to your city with”, he brought.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَتِ السِّتُّ دُنْيَا مِنْ كَلَامِ الْعَجُوزِ وَقَالَتْ أَخْزَاكِ اللَّهُ يَاعَجُوزَ النَّحْسِ إِنَّكِ خَرِفْتِ وَمَا بَقِيَ لَكِ عَقْلٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikati al-sittu dunyā min kalāmi al-ʿajūzi wa-qālat akhzāki allāhu yā ʿajūza al-naḥsi innaki kharifti wa-mā baqiya laki ʿaqlun
sentences.l: And the Lady Dunyā laughed at the speech of the old woman and said: May God disgrace you, O old-woman of the ill-omen! Indeed you have become-senile, and there did not remain to you a mind.
sentences.i: The Lady Dunyā laughed at the old woman's words and said, “God shame you, you ill-omened old woman! You have gone soft in the head, and there is no sense left in you.”
sentences.n: ʿajūz al-naḥs, “old woman of ill luck”, a stock insult.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ هَاتِى الْقُمَاشَ حَتَّى أَنْظُرَهُ نَظَرًا جَيِّدًا فَأَعْطَتْهَا إِيَّاهُ فَنَظَرَتْهُ ثَانِيًا فَرَأَتْهُ قَلِيلًا وَثَمَنَهُ كَثِيرًا فَأَعْجَبَهَا لِأَنَّهَا مَارَأَتْ فِي عُمْرِهَا مِثْلَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat hātī al-qumāsha ḥattā anẓurahu naẓaran jayyidan fa-aʿṭathā iyyāhu fa-naẓarathu thāniyan fa-raʾathu qalīlan wa-thamanahu kathīran fa-aʿjabahā li-annahā mā raʾat fī ʿumrihā mithlahu
sentences.l: Then she said: Give the cloth, so that I look at it a looking good. So she gave her it, and she looked at it a second (time), and saw it little and its price much; and it pleased her, because she had not seen in her life its like.
sentences.i: Then she said, “Give me the cloth, so that I can look at it properly.” The old woman gave it to her, and she looked at it again, and saw that it was light in the hand and heavy in price; and she liked it, for she had never in her life seen anything like it.
sentences.n: qalīlan wa-thamanahu kathīran, “little, and its price much”: a stock phrase for precious goods, small in bulk and great in value. The print spells hātī with a final ى (هاتى).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّهُ قُمَاشٌ مَلِيحٌ فَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْعَجُوزُ يَاسَيِّدَتِي وَاللَّهِ لَوْرَأَيْتِ صَاحِبَهُ لَعَرَفْتِ أَنَّهُ أَحْسَنُ مَنْ يَكُونُ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-allāhi innahu qumāshun malīḥun fa-qālat lahā al-ʿajūzu yā sayyidatī wa-allāhi law raʾayti ṣāḥibahu la-ʿarafti annahu aḥsanu man yakūnu ʿalā wajhi al-arḍi
sentences.l: And she said: By God, indeed it (is) cloth pretty. And the old woman said to her: O my lady, by God, if you saw its owner, you would know that he (is) the most beautiful of who is on the face of the earth.
sentences.i: “By God,” she said, “it is lovely cloth.” The old woman said to her, “My lady, by God, if you saw its owner you would know he is the most beautiful man on the face of the earth.”
sentences.n: The print runs law raʾayti together and marks its feminine -ti with a kasra (لورأيتِ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا السِّتُّ دُنْيَا هَلْ كُنْتِ سَأَلْتِهِ إِنْ كَانَ لَهُ حَاجَةٌ يُعْلِمُنَا بِهَا فَنَقْضِيهَا لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-sittu dunyā hal kunti saʾaltihi in kāna lahu ḥājatun yuʿlimunā bihā fa-naqḍīhā lahu
sentences.l: And the Lady Dunyā said to her: Had you asked him, if there is to him a need, (that) he inform us of it, so we fulfil it for him?
sentences.i: The Lady Dunyā said to her, “Did you ask him whether there is anything he needs? He should let us know, and we will see to it for him.”
sentences.n: aʿlamahu bi-, “to inform someone of”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُ وَقَدْ هَزَّتْ رَأْسَهَا حَفِظَ اللَّهُ فِرَاسَتَكِ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ لَهُ حَاجَةً لَاعَدِمْتُ مَعْرِفَتَكِ وَهَلْ أَحَدٌ يَسْلَمُ وَيَخْلُو مِنْ حَاجَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu wa-qad hazzat raʾsahā ḥafiẓa allāhu firāsataki wa-allāhi inna lahu ḥājatan lā ʿadimtu maʿrifataki wa-hal aḥadun yaslamu wa-yakhlū min ḥājatin
sentences.l: And the old woman said, and she had shaken her head: May God preserve your insight! By God, indeed to him (is) a need — may I not lose your acquaintance! And is anyone safe and free from a need?
sentences.i: The old woman shook her head and said, “God preserve your shrewdness! By God, he does have a need — may I never be without you! — and is there anyone who has no need at all?”
sentences.n: firāsa, “insight, the gift of reading people”. lā ʿadimtu maʿrifataki, “may I not be deprived of knowing you”: a wish in the perfect after lā, a courteous aside.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا السِّتُّ دُنْيَا اذْهَبِي إِلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمِي عَلَيْهِ وَقُولِي لَهُ شَرَّفْتَ بِقُدُومِكَ أَرْضَنَا وَمَدِينَتَنَا وَمَهْمَا كَانَ لَكَ مِنَ الْحَوَائِجِ قَضَيْنَاهَا لَكَ عَلَى الرَّأْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-sittu dunyā idhhabī ilayhi wa-sallimī ʿalayhi wa-qūlī lahu sharrafta bi-qudūmika arḍanā wa-madīnatanā wa-mahmā kāna laka mina al-ḥawāʾiji qaḍaynāhā laka ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayni
sentences.l: And the Lady Dunyā said to her: Go to him and greet him and say to him: You have honoured with your coming our land and our city; and whatever there is to you of the needs, we will fulfil them for you, on the head and the eye.
sentences.i: The Lady Dunyā said to her, “Go to him, greet him and tell him: ‘Your coming has honoured our land and our city, and whatever you need, we will see to it gladly.’”
sentences.n: ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayn, “on the head and the eye”: “with the greatest pleasure”. bi-qudūmika, “by your coming”: bi- of means. The perfect qaḍaynāhā after mahmā has future sense, “we will fulfil”.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَتِ الْعَجُوزُ إِلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فِى الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿati al-ʿajūzu ilā tāji al-mulūki fī al-waqti
sentences.l: And the old woman returned to Tāj al-Mulūk in the time.
sentences.i: The old woman went straight back to Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.n: fī al-waqt, “at once”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا طَارَ قَلْبُهُ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ وَالسُّرُورِ وَقَامَ لَهَا قَائِمًا عَلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَأَخَذَ يَدَهَا وَأَجْلَسَهَا إِلَى جَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā ṭāra qalbuhu mina al-faraḥi wa-al-surūri wa-qāma lahā qāʾiman ʿalā qadamayhi wa-akhadha yadahā wa-ajlasahā ilā jānibihi
sentences.l: And when he saw her, his heart flew from the joy and the gladness, and he stood for her, standing on his two feet, and took her hand and seated her at his side.
sentences.i: When he saw her, his heart leapt for joy and gladness; he rose to his feet for her, took her hand and sat her down beside him.
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for ilā (الى), “to, beside”, corrected here; the lām has dropped out.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَلَسَتْ وَاسْتَرَاحَتْ أَخْبَرَتْهُ بِمَا قَالَتْهُ لَهَا السِّتُّ دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jalasat wa-istarāḥat akhbarathu bi-mā qālathu lahā al-sittu dunyā
sentences.l: And when she sat and rested, she informed him of what the Lady Dunyā said to her.
sentences.i: When she had sat and rested, she told him what the Lady Dunyā had said to her.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to tell of”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ ذَلِكَ فَرِحَ غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ وَاتَّسَعَ صَدْرُهُ وَانْشَرَحَ وَدَخَلَ فِي قَلْبِهِ سُرُورٌ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ قَدْ قُضِيَتْ حَاجَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa dhālika fariḥa ghāyata al-faraḥi wa-ittasaʿa ṣadruhu wa-insharaḥa wa-dakhala fī qalbihi surūrun wa-qāla fī nafsihi qad quḍiyat ḥājatī
sentences.l: And when he heard that, he rejoiced the utmost of the joy, and his breast widened and expanded, and there entered into his heart gladness, and he said in himself: My need has been fulfilled.
sentences.i: When he heard it he was overjoyed; his heart swelled and opened, gladness came into it, and he said to himself, “What I wanted is as good as done.”
sentences.n: The print has وانسع, a misprint for wa-ittasaʿa (واتسع), “and (his breast) widened”, corrected here; a dot is misplaced. A widened breast is a glad heart. The print marks quḍiyat with its own vowels (قُضيتْ).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْعَجُوزِ لَعَلَّكِ أَنْ تَأْخُذِى لَهَا مِنْ عِنْدِي رِسَالَةً وَتَأْتِينِي بِجَوَابِهَا فَقَالَتْ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: thumma qāla li-al-ʿajūzi laʿallaki an taʾkhudhī lahā min ʿindī risālatan wa-taʾtīnī bi-jawābihā fa-qālat samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: Then he said to the old woman: Perhaps you (might) take to her from me a message, and bring me its answer? And she said: Hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: Then he said to the old woman, “Would you perhaps take a letter from me to her, and bring me back her answer?” She said, “With hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: laʿallaki an, “perhaps you”: Middle Arabic adds an before the verb after laʿalla. atā bi-, “to bring”. The print spells taʾkhudhī with a final ى (تاخذى).

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ لِعَزِيزٍ ائْتِنِي بِدَوَاةٍ وَقِرْطَاسٍ وَقَلَمٍ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ فَلَمَّا أَتَاهُ بِتِلْكَ الْأَدَوَاتِ أَخَذَ الْقَلَمَ بِيَدِهِ وَكَتَبَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāla li-ʿazīzin iʾtinī bi-dawātin wa-qirṭāsin wa-qalamin min nuḥāsin fa-lammā atāhu bi-tilka al-adawāti akhadha al-qalama bi-yadihi wa-kataba hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: So at that he said to ʿAzīz: Bring me an inkwell and paper and a pen of brass. And when he brought him those implements, he took the pen in his hand and wrote these verses — poetry:
sentences.i: Then he said to ʿAzīz, “Bring me an inkwell, paper and a brass pen.” When ʿAzīz had brought them, he took the pen in his hand and wrote these verses:
sentences.n: shiʿr, “poetry”, is the print's label announcing verse; it is not part of the sentence. A pen “of brass” is a metal reed-shaped pen. iʾtinī bi-, atāhu bi-: atā bi- is “to bring”.

sentences.t:
كَتَبْتُ اِلَيْكَ يَاسُؤْلِي كِتَابًا * بِمَا اَلْقَاهُ مِنْ اَلَمِ الْفِرَاقِ
فَاَوَّلُ سَطْرِهِ نَارُ بِقَلْبِي * وَثَانِيْهِ غَرَامِي وَاشْتِيَاقِي
وَثَالِثُهُ فَنَى عُمْرِي وَصَبْرِي * وَرَابِعُهُ جَمِيعُ الْوَجْدِ بَاقِي
وَخَامِسُهُ مَتَى عَيْنِى تَرَاكُمْ * وَسَادِسُهُ مَتَى يَوْمُ التَّلَاقِيْ
sentences.tr:
katabtu ilayka yā suʾlī kitāban * bi-mā alqāhu min alami al-firāqi
fa-awwalu saṭrihi nāru bi-qalbī * wa-thānīhi gharāmī wa-ishtiyāqī
wa-thālithuhu fanā ʿumrī wa-ṣabrī * wa-rābiʿuhu jamīʿu al-wajdi bāqī
wa-khāmisuhu matā ʿaynī tarākum * wa-sādisuhu matā yawmu al-talāqī
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. bi-mā, “with what, of what”: bi- gives the letter's contents. The print points nāru, “fire”, with a bare ḍamma where nārun is expected, and writes fanā for faniya, “perished” (فَنَى). tarākum, “see you” (plural): love poetry often addresses the beloved in the plural, and in the masculine.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ فِي إِمْضَائِهِ أَنَّ هَذَا الْكِتَابَ مِنْ أَسِيرِ الْأَشْوَاقِ * الْمَسْجُونِ فِي سِجْنِ الِاشْتِيَاقِ * الَّذِي لَيْسَ لَهُ مِنْهُ إِطْلَاقٌ * إِلَّا بِالْوِصَالِ وَالتَّلَاقِ * بَعْدَ الْبُعْدِ وَالْفِرَاقِ * لِأَنَّهُ يُقَاسِى مِنْ فُرْقَةِ الْأَحْبَابِ * أَلِيمَ الْوَجْدِ وَالْعَذَابِ *
sentences.tr: thumma kataba fī imḍāʾihi anna hādhā al-kitāba min asīri al-ashwāqi * al-masjūni fī sijni al-ishtiyāqi * alladhī laysa lahu minhu iṭlāqun * illā bi-al-wiṣāli wa-al-talāqi * baʿda al-buʿdi wa-al-firāqi * li-annahu yuqāsī min furqati al-aḥbābi * alīma al-wajdi wa-al-ʿadhābi *
sentences.l: Then he wrote in its signing-off that this letter (is) from the captive of the yearnings, * the imprisoned in the prison of the longing, * who has not from it a release * except by the union and the meeting * after the distance and the parting, * because he suffers from the separation of the loved-ones * painful ardour and torment.
sentences.i: Then, where he signed it, he wrote: This letter is from the captive of yearning, * the prisoner in the jail of longing, * who has no release from it * but in union and meeting * after distance and parting, * for he suffers, from the beloved's departing, * the pain of passion and tormenting.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose (sajʿ), which the print marks off with stars: -āq five times, then -āb. imḍāʾ, “signature”, here the closing lines above the signature. bi-al-wiṣāl, “by union”: bi- of means. al-talāq is al-talāqī, “meeting”, shortened for the rhyme. The print spells yuqāsī with a final ى (يقاسى).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَفَاضَ دَمْعَ الْعَيْنِ وَكَتَبَ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma afāḍa damʿa al-ʿayni wa-kataba hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then he poured-forth the tear of the eye and wrote these two verses:
sentences.i: Then, his tears flowing, he wrote these two lines:

sentences.t:
كَتَبْتُ اِلَيْكَ وَالْعَبَرَاتُ تَجْرِي * وَدَمْعُ الْعَيْنِ لَيْسَ لَهُ انْقِطَاعُ
وَلَسْتُ بَآيِسٍ مِنْ فَضْلِ رَبِّي * عَسَى يَوْمٌ يَكُونُ بِهِ اِجْتِمَاعُ
sentences.tr:
katabtu ilayka wa-al-ʿabarātu tajrī * wa-damʿu al-ʿayni laysa lahu inqiṭāʿu
wa-lastu bi-āyisin min faḍli rabbī * ʿasā yawmun yakūnu bihi ijtimāʿu
sentences.l:
I wrote to you and the tears (are) running, * and the tear of the eye, there is not to it a ceasing;
And I am not despairing of the bounty of my Lord: * perhaps a day (will) be, in it a coming-together.
sentences.i:
I wrote to you with my tears still running, * and the weeping of my eyes knows no end;
Yet I do not despair of my Lord's bounty: * perhaps a day will come that brings us together.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. bi-āyisin, “despairing”: bi- after a negative (lastu) only strengthens it. The final -u of inqiṭāʿu and ijtimāʿu is the rhyme vowel. ʿasā, “perhaps”, here with a noun: “perhaps a day …”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَوَى الْكِتَابَ وَخَتَمَهُ وَأَعْطَاهُ لِلْعَجُوزِ وَقَالَ لَهَا أَوْصِلِيهِ إِلَى السِّتِّ دُنْيَا فَقَالَتْ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: thumma ṭawā al-kitāba wa-khatamahu wa-aʿṭāhu li-al-ʿajūzi wa-qāla lahā awṣilīhi ilā al-sitti dunyā fa-qālat samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: Then he folded the letter and sealed it and gave it to the old woman, and said to her: Deliver it to the Lady Dunyā. And she said: Hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: Then he folded the letter, sealed it and gave it to the old woman, saying, “Take it to the Lady Dunyā.” She said, “With hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: aʿṭāhu li-, “he gave it to”: Middle Arabic marks the receiver with li- where Classical has a second object.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَعْطَاهَا أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ وَقَالَ يَا أُمِّي اقْبَلِي هَذِهِ هَدِيَّةً مِنِّي عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمَحَبَّةِ فَأَخَذَتْهَا مِنْهُ وَدَعَتْ لَهُ وَانْصَرَفَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma aʿṭāhā alfa dīnārin wa-qāla yā ummī iqbalī hādhihi hadiyyatan minnī ʿalā sabīli al-maḥabbati fa-akhadhathā minhu wa-daʿat lahu wa-inṣarafat
sentences.l: Then he gave her a thousand dinars and said: O my mother, accept this, a gift from me by way of the love. And she took it from him and prayed for him and departed.
sentences.i: Then he gave her a thousand dinars and said, “Mother, accept this as a gift from me, in friendship.” She took it from him, called down blessings on him and went away.
sentences.n: yā ummī, “O my mother”, a polite address to an older woman. daʿā lahu, “to pray for someone”: li- marks the one prayed for.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ مَاشِيَةً حَتَّى دَخَلَتْ عَلَى السِّتِّ دُنْيَا فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهَا قَالَتْ لَهَا يَا دَادَتِي إِيشْ طَلَبَ مِنَ الْحَوَائِجِ حَتَّى نَقْضِيَهَا لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal māshiyatan ḥattā dakhalat ʿalā al-sitti dunyā fa-lammā raʾathā qālat lahā yā dādatī īsh ṭalaba mina al-ḥawāʾiji ḥattā naqḍiyahā lahu
sentences.l: And she did not cease walking until she entered upon the Lady Dunyā; and when she saw her, she said to her: O my nurse, what did he ask of the needs, so that we fulfil them for him?
sentences.i: She walked on until she came in to the Lady Dunyā, who, as soon as she saw her, said, “Nanny, what does he need, so that we can see to it for him?”
sentences.n: īsh, “what?”, colloquial (from ayy shayʾ, “which thing”).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا سَيِّدَتِي إِنَّهُ قَدْ أَرْسَلَ مَعِي هَذَا الْكِتَابَ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ مَا فِيهِ ثُمَّ نَاوَلَتْهَا الْكِتَابَ فَأَخَذَتْهُ وَقَرَأَتْهُ وَفَهِمَتْ مَعْنَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā yā sayyidatī innahu qad arsala maʿī hādhā al-kitāba wa-lā aʿlamu mā fīhi thumma nāwalathā al-kitāba fa-akhadhathu wa-qaraʾathu wa-fahimat maʿnāhu
sentences.l: And she said to her: O my lady, indeed he has sent with me this letter, and I do not know what (is) in it. Then she handed her the letter, and she took it and read it and understood its meaning.
sentences.i: She said to her, “My lady, he has sent this letter with me, and I do not know what is in it.” Then she handed her the letter, and Dunyā took it, read it and understood it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ مِنْ أَيْنَ إِلَى أَيْنَ حَتَّى يُرَاسِلَنِي هَذَا التَّاجِرُ وَيُكَاتِبَنِي
sentences.tr: thumma qālat min ayna ilā ayna ḥattā yurāsilanī hādhā al-tājiru wa-yukātibanī
sentences.l: Then she said: From where to where, that this merchant should send-messages-to me and write-to me?
sentences.i: Then she said, “Who does he think he is, and who does he think I am, that this merchant should send me messages and write to me?”
sentences.n: min ayna ilā ayna, “from where to where?”: an indignant question about the distance between his station and hers.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَطَمَتْ وَجْهَهَا وَقَالَتْ مِنْ أَيْنَ كُنَّا حَتَّى اتَّصَلْنَا وَوَصَلْنَا إِلَى السُّوقَةِ أَوَّاهْ أَوَّاهْ
sentences.tr: thumma laṭamat wajhahā wa-qālat min ayna kunnā ḥattā ittaṣalnā wa-waṣalnā ilā al-sūqati awwāh awwāh
sentences.l: Then she slapped her face and said: From where were we, until we became-connected and arrived to the common-folk? Alas, alas!
sentences.i: Then she slapped her own face and said, “How high we stood — and now we have come down to this, to dealings with the common people! Alas, alas!”
sentences.n: al-sūqa, “the common people, subjects” (not royalty). awwāh, “alas!”, printed with its doubling mark (اوّاه).

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ لَوْلَا خَوْفِي مِنَ اللَّهِ لَقَتَلْتُهُ وَصَلَبْتُهُ عَلَى دُكَّانِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat wa-allāhi lawlā khawfī mina allāhi la-qataltuhu wa-ṣalabtuhu ʿalā dukkānihi
sentences.l: And she said: By God, were it not for my fear of God, I would have killed him and crucified him upon his shop!
sentences.i: And she said, “By God, if it were not that I fear God, I would have him killed and crucified on his own shop!”
sentences.n: ṣalaba, “to crucify”: in the Nights, to hang up or nail a body on a post for public display.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُ وَإِيشْ فِي هَذَا الْكِتَابِ حَتَّى إِنَّهُ أَزْعَجَ قَلْبَكِ وَغَيَّرَ خَاطِرَكِ يَا تُرَى هَلْ فِيهِ شِكَايَةُ مَظْلِمَةٍ أَوْفِيهِ طَلَبُ ثَمَنِ الْقُمَاشِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu wa-īsh fī hādhā al-kitābi ḥattā innahu azʿaja qalbaki wa-ghayyara khāṭiraki yā turā hal fīhi shikāyatu maẓlimatin aw fīhi ṭalabu thamani al-qumāshi
sentences.l: And the old woman said: And what (is) in this letter, so that indeed it disturbed your heart and changed your mind? O do-you-see, is there in it a complaint of a wrong, or in it a demand of the price of the cloth?
sentences.i: The old woman said, “And what is in this letter, that it has upset you so and put you out of temper? Is there a complaint in it of some wrong done him, I wonder, or is he asking for the price of the cloth?”
sentences.n: yā turā, “O, is it seen?”, colloquial for “I wonder”. maẓlima, “a wrong suffered, a grievance”. The print runs aw fīhi together (اوفيه).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا وَيْلَكِ مَا فِيهِ ذَلِكَ وَمَا فِيهِ إِلَّا كَلَامُ عِشْقٍ وَمَحَبَّةٍ وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ مِنْكِ وَإِلَّا فَمِنْ أَيْنَ هَذَا الشَّيْطَانُ كَانَ يَعْرِفُنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā waylaki mā fīhi dhālika wa-mā fīhi illā kalāmu ʿishqin wa-maḥabbatin wa-hādhā kulluhu minki wa-illā fa-min ayna hādhā al-shayṭānu kāna yaʿrifunī
sentences.l: And she said to her: Woe to you! There is not in it that, and there is not in it except speech of passion and love; and this all (is) from you — and otherwise, then from where was this devil knowing me?
sentences.i: She said to her, “Damn you, there is nothing of the kind in it! There is nothing in it but words of passion and love, and all of this is your doing — how else would this devil know who I am?”
sentences.n: waylaki, “woe to you!”. wa-illā, “and if not, otherwise”. The print marks the feminine -ki of minki with a kasra.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْعَجُوزُ يَا سَيِّدَتِى أَنْتِ قَاعِدَةٌ فِي قَصْرِكِ الْعَالِي وَمَا يَصِلُ إِلَيْكِ أَحَدٌ وَلَا الطَّيْرُ الطَّائِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā al-ʿajūzu yā sayyidatī anti qāʿidatun fī qaṣriki al-ʿālī wa-mā yaṣilu ilayki aḥadun wa-lā al-ṭayru al-ṭāʾiru
sentences.l: And the old woman said to her: O my lady, you (are) sitting in your palace the high, and no one reaches to you, nor the bird the flying.
sentences.i: The old woman said to her, “My lady, you sit in your lofty palace where no one can come near you — not even a bird on the wing.”
sentences.n: The print marks the feminine endings here with kasras (انتِ, قصركِ, اليكِ) and spells sayyidatī with a final ى.

sentences.t: سَلَامَتُكِ وَسَلَامَةُ شَبَابِكِ مِنَ اللَّوْمِ وَالْعِتَابِ وَمَا عَلَيْكِ مِنْ نَبِيحِ الْكِلَابِ فَأَنْتِ سَيِّدَةٌ بِنْتُ سَيِّدٍ
sentences.tr: salāmatuki wa-salāmatu shabābiki mina al-lawmi wa-al-ʿitābi wa-mā ʿalayki min nabīḥi al-kilābi fa-anti sayyidatun bintu sayyidin
sentences.l: Your safety and the safety of your youth from the blame and the reproach! And there is not upon you (anything) from the barking of the dogs; for you (are) a lady, daughter of a lord.
sentences.i: May you and your youth be kept safe from blame and reproach! And the barking of dogs is nothing to you, for you are a lady and a lord's daughter.
sentences.n: salāmatuki …, “your safety!”: an exclamatory wish with no verb, “may you be safe from”. mā ʿalayki min, “there is nothing on you from”, “you need not mind”. lawm and ʿitāb, kilāb: a touch of rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَا تُوْاخِذِينِى حَيْثُ جِئْتُ إِلَيْكِ بِهَذَا الْكِتَابِ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ بِمَافِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lā tuʾākhidhīnī ḥaythu jiʾtu ilayki bi-hādhā al-kitābi wa-lā aʿlamu bi-mā fīhi
sentences.l: So do not blame me where I have come to you with this letter, and I do not know of what (is) in it.
sentences.i: So do not hold it against me that I brought you this letter; I did not know what was in it.
sentences.n: ḥaythu, “where”, here “in that, because”: a Middle Arabic use. jāʾa bi-, “to bring”. ʿalima bi-, “to know of”. The print sets a sukūn-like mark over the wāw of tuʾākhidhīnī (توْاخذينى), where the hamza would go; kept, and read tuʾākhidhīnī. It runs bi-mā fīhi together.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنَّ الرَّأْيَ أَنْ تَرُدِّي إِلَيْهِ جَوَابًا وَتُهَدِّدِيهِ فِيهِ بِالْقَتْلِ وَتَنْهَيْهِ عَنْ هَذَا الْهَذَيَانِ فَإِنَّهُ يَنْتَهِي وَلَا يَعُودُ إِلَى مِثْلِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinna al-raʾya an taruddī ilayhi jawāban wa-tuhaddidīhi fīhi bi-al-qatli wa-tanhayhi ʿan hādhā al-hadhayāni fa-innahu yantahī wa-lā yaʿūdu ilā mithli dhālika
sentences.l: But the opinion (is) that you return to him an answer and threaten him in it with the killing and forbid him from this raving; for he will desist and not return to the like of that.
sentences.i: But my advice is that you send him an answer, threaten him in it with death and forbid him this nonsense; then he will stop and not do such a thing again.
sentences.n: haddada bi-, “to threaten with”: bi- marks the threat.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ السَّيِّدَةُ دُنْيَا أَخَافُ أَنْ أُكَاتِبَهُ فَيَطْمَعَ فِيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-sayyidatu dunyā akhāfu an ukātibahu fa-yaṭmaʿa fiyya
sentences.l: And the Lady Dunyā said: I fear that I write-to him and he covet me.
sentences.i: The Lady Dunyā said, “I am afraid that if I write to him he will set his hopes on me.”
sentences.n: ṭamiʿa fī, “to covet, to set one's hopes on”. The print marks fiyya, “on me”, with its own doubling mark (فيّ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْعَجُوزُ إِنَّهُ إِذَا سَمِعَ التَّهْدِيدَ وَالْوَعِيدَ رَجَعَ عَمَّا هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ʿajūzu innahu idhā samiʿa al-tahdīda wa-al-waʿīda rajaʿa ʿammā huwa fīhi
sentences.l: And the old woman said: Indeed he, if he hears the threatening and the menace, will return from what he (is) in.
sentences.i: The old woman said, “Once he hears threats and menaces, he will give up what he is about.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ عَلَيَّ بِدَوَاةٍ وَقِرْطَاسٍ وَقَلَمٍ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ فَلَمَّا أَحْضَرُوا لَهَا تِلْكَ الْأَدَوَاتِ كَتَبَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ʿalayya bi-dawātin wa-qirṭāsin wa-qalamin min nuḥāsin fa-lammā aḥḍarū lahā tilka al-adawāti katabat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And she said: Upon me with an inkwell and paper and a pen of brass! And when they brought to her those implements, she wrote these verses:
sentences.i: She said, “Bring me an inkwell, paper and a brass pen!” When they had brought them, she wrote these verses:
sentences.n: ʿalayya bi-, “on me with …!”: an order to fetch something. The print marks ʿalayya with its own doubling mark (عليّ).

sentences.t:
يَامُدَّعِي الْحُبِّ وَالْبَلْوَى مَعَ السَّهَرِ * وَمَا يُلَاقِيهِ مِنْ وَجْدٍ وَمِنْ فِكَرِ
اَتَطْلُبُ الْوَصْلَ يَامَغْرُورُ مِنْ قَمَرٍ * وَهَلْ يَنَالُ الْمُنَى شَخْصٌ مِنَ الْقَمَرِ
اِنِّي نَصَحْتُكَ عَمَّا اَنْتَ طَالِبُهُ * فَاقْصُرْ فَاِنَّكَ فِي هٰذَا عَلَى خَطَرِ
وَاِنْ رَجَعْتَ اِلَى هٰذَا الْكَلَامِ فَقَدْ * اَتَاكَ مِنِّي عَذَابُ زَائِدُ الضَّرَرِ
وَحَقِّ مَنْ خَلَقَ الْاِنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ * وَمَنْ اَنَارَ ضِيَاوَ الشَّمْسِ وَالْقَدَرِ
لَئِنْ رَجَعْتَ اِلَى مَا اَنْتَ ذَاكِرُهُ * لَاُصْلِبَنَّكَ فِي جِذْعٍ مِنَ الشَّجَرِ
sentences.tr:
yā muddaʿiya al-ḥubbi wa-al-balwā maʿa al-sahari * wa-mā yulāqīhi min wajdin wa-min fikari
a-taṭlubu al-waṣla yā maghrūru min qamarin * wa-hal yanālu al-munā shakhṣun mina al-qamari
innī naṣaḥtuka ʿammā anta ṭālibuhu * fa-aqṣur fa-innaka fī hādhā ʿalā khaṭari
wa-in rajaʿta ilā hādhā al-kalāmi fa-qad * atāka minnī ʿadhābu zāʾidu al-ḍarari
wa-ḥaqqi man khalaqa al-insāna min ʿalaqin * wa-man anāra ḍiyāwa al-shamsi wa-al-qadari
laʾin rajaʿta ilā mā anta dhākiruhu * la-uṣlibannaka fī jidhʿin mina al-shajari
sentences.l:
O claimer of the love and the affliction with the sleeplessness, * and what he meets of ardour and of thoughts!
Do you seek the union, O deluded one, from a moon? * And does a person attain the wishes from the moon?
Indeed I have advised you against what you (are) seeking it; * so desist, for you, in this, (are) upon danger.
And if you return to this speech, then indeed * there has come to you from me a torment exceeding (in) the harm.
By the right of who created man from a clot, * and who lit the light of the sun and the destiny:
If you return to what you (are) mentioning it, * I will surely crucify you on a trunk of the trees!
sentences.i:
You who claim to love, and boast your suffering and sleepless nights, * your ardour and the fancies that you meet:
Do you, deluded fool, seek union with the moon? * Has anyone yet had his wish of the moon?
I warn you now: give up what you are seeking; * stop, for in this you put yourself in danger.
And if you come back to this talk again, * then a punishment from me will come on you, past bearing.
By Him who made man from a clot of blood, * and kindled the light of the sun and of destiny,
If you return to what you speak of here, * I will crucify you on a tree-trunk, I swear!
sentences.n: The print has بامغرور, a misprint for yā maghrūru (يامغرور), “O deluded one”, corrected here; the dots of yāʾ became the one dot of bāʾ. Apart from this word the verse is given exactly as printed, with its vowels. The print writes ḍiyāʾ, “light”, as ضِيَاوَ, with wāw for the hamza. It has al-qadar, “fate, destiny”, where al-qamar, “the moon”, would fit the sun better; but the poem has already rhymed twice on qamar, so the print is kept, and our English gives the poet's word. min ʿalaq, “from a clot”, is Qurʾānic (96:2). la-uṣlibannaka, “I will surely crucify you”, is printed with a ḍamma on the first letter; the usual forms are la-aṣlibannaka (ṣalaba, yaṣlibu) or, as in the Qurʾān (7:124), la-uṣallibannaka; the print's ḍamma points to a form IV that the dictionaries do not record. Dunyā addresses him in the masculine singular throughout, as he is.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَوَتِ الْكِتَابَ وَأَعْطَتْهُ الْعَجُوزَ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا أَعْطِيهِ لَهُ وَقُولِي لَهُ كُفَّ عَنْ هَذَا الْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṭawati al-kitāba wa-aʿṭathu al-ʿajūza wa-qālat lahā aʿṭīhi lahu wa-qūlī lahu kuffa ʿan hādhā al-kalāmi
sentences.l: Then she folded the letter and gave it the old woman and said to her: Give it to him, and say to him: Refrain from this speech.
sentences.i: Then she folded the letter, gave it to the old woman and said to her, “Give it to him, and tell him: ‘Stop this talk.’”
sentences.n: kaffa ʿan, “to refrain from”; the print marks kuffa with its doubling mark (كفّ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً ثُمَّ أَخَذَتِ الْكِتَابَ وَهِيَ فَرْحَانَةٌ وَمَضَتْ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهَا وَبَاتَتْ فِي بَيْتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan thumma akhadhati al-kitāba wa-hiya farḥānatun wa-maḍat ilā manzilihā wa-bātat fī baytihā
sentences.l: And she said to her: Hearing and obedience. Then she took the letter, and she (was) glad, and went to her lodging and spent-the-night in her house.
sentences.i: She said to her, “With hearing and obedience.” Then she took the letter, delighted, and went home and spent the night in her own house.
sentences.n: farḥāna, “glad”, a colloquial form.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ تَوَجَّهَتْ إِلَى دُكَّانِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَوَجَدَتْهُ فِي انْتِظَارِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu tawajjahat ilā dukkāni tāji al-mulūki fa-wajadathu fī intiẓārihā
sentences.l: And when the morning became-morning, she directed-herself to the shop of Tāj al-Mulūk, and found him in waiting for her.
sentences.i: When morning came she made her way to Tāj al-Mulūk's shop, and found him waiting for her.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا كَادَ أَنْ يَطِيرَ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ فَلَمَّا قَرُبَتْ مِنْهُ نَهَضَ إِلَيْهَا قَائِمًا وَأَقْعَدَهَا بِجَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā kāda an yaṭīra mina al-faraḥi fa-lammā qarubat minhu nahaḍa ilayhā qāʾiman wa-aqʿadahā bi-jānibihi
sentences.l: And when he saw her, he almost flew from the joy; and when she came-near to him, he rose to her standing and seated her at his side.
sentences.i: When he saw her he nearly flew for joy; and when she came up to him he rose and went to meet her, and sat her down beside him.
sentences.n: bi-jānibihi, “at his side”: bi- of place.

sentences.t: فَأَخْرَجَتْ لَهُ الْوَرَقَةَ وَنَاوَلَتْهُ إِيَّاهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهُ اقْرَأْ مَا فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhrajat lahu al-waraqata wa-nāwalathu iyyāhā wa-qālat lahu iqraʾ mā fīhā
sentences.l: And she brought out for him the paper and handed him it, and said to him: Read what (is) in it.
sentences.i: She took out the paper, handed it to him and said, “Read what it says.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ السَّيِّدَةَ دُنْيَا لَمَّا قَرَأَتْ كِتَابَكَ اغْتَاظَتْ وَلَكِنَّنِي لَاطَفْتُهَا وَمَازَحْتُهَا حَتَّى أَضْحَكْتُهَا وَرَقَّتْ لَكَ وَرَدَّتْ لَكَ الْجَوَابَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahu inna al-sayyidata dunyā lammā qaraʾat kitābaka ightāẓat wa-lākinnanī lāṭaftuhā wa-māzaḥtuhā ḥattā aḍḥaktuhā wa-raqqat laka wa-raddat laka al-jawāba
sentences.l: Then she said to him: Indeed the Lady Dunyā, when she read your letter, became-angry; but I coaxed her and joked-with her until I made her laugh, and she softened to you and returned to you the answer.
sentences.i: Then she said to him, “When the Lady Dunyā read your letter she was furious; but I coaxed her and teased her until I made her laugh, and she softened towards you and sent you an answer.”
sentences.n: raqqa li-, “to soften towards, to pity”.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَأَمَرَ عَزِيزًا أَنْ يُعْطِيَهَا أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-shakarahā tāju al-mulūki ʿalā dhālika wa-amara ʿazīzan an yuʿṭiyahā alfa dīnārin
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk thanked her for that, and ordered ʿAzīz that he give her a thousand dinars.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk thanked her for it, and told ʿAzīz to give her a thousand dinars.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ قَرَأَ الْكِتَابَ وَفَهِمَهُ وَبَكَى بُكَاءًا شَدِيدًا فَرَقَّ لَهُ قَلْبُ الْعَجُوزِ وَعَظُمَ عَلَيْهَا بُكَاؤُهُ وَشَكْوَاهُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu qaraʾa al-kitāba wa-fahimahu wa-bakā bukāʾan shadīdan fa-raqqa lahu qalbu al-ʿajūzi wa-ʿaẓuma ʿalayhā bukāʾuhu wa-shakwāhu
sentences.l: Then he read the letter and understood it, and wept a weeping strong; and the heart of the old woman softened to him, and his weeping and his complaint were great upon her.
sentences.i: Then he read the letter and understood it, and wept bitterly; the old woman's heart was moved for him, and his weeping and lament weighed on her.
sentences.n: The print spells bukāʾan with an extra alif after the hamza (بكاءا). ʿaẓuma ʿalā, “to weigh heavily on”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ فِي هَذِهِ الْوَرَقَةِ حَتَّى أَبْكَاكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahu yā waladī wa-ayyu shayʾin fī hādhihi al-waraqati ḥattā abkāka
sentences.l: Then she said to him: O my son, and what thing (is) in this paper, so that it made you weep?
sentences.i: Then she said to him, “My son, what is in this paper that it has made you weep?”
sentences.n: The print has فالت, a misprint for qālat (قالت), “she said”, corrected here; one dot for two.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا إِنَّهَا تُهَدِّدُنِي بِالْقَتْلِ وَالصَّلْبِ وَتَنْهَانِي عَنْ مُرَاسَلَتِهَا وَإِنْ لَمْ أُرَاسِلْهَا يَكُونُ مَوْتِي خَيْرًا مِنْ حَيٰوتِي فَخُذِي جَوَابَ كِتَابِهَا وَدَعِيهَا تَفْعَلُ مَا تُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā innahā tuhaddidunī bi-al-qatli wa-al-ṣalbi wa-tanhānī ʿan murāsalatihā wa-in lam urāsilhā yakūnu mawtī khayran min ḥayātī fa-khudhī jawāba kitābihā wa-daʿīhā tafʿalu mā turīdu
sentences.l: And he said to her: Indeed she threatens me with the killing and the crucifying, and forbids me from corresponding-with her; and if I do not correspond-with her, my death will be better than my life. So take the answer to her letter, and let her do what she wants.
sentences.i: He said to her, “She threatens me with death and crucifixion and forbids me to write to her; but if I do not write to her, I would be better dead than alive. So take her the answer to her letter, and let her do what she likes.”
sentences.n: The print spells ḥayāt with wāw (حيوتي), the old Qurʾānic spelling; the small alif over the yāʾ is ours, to show the long vowel. yakūnu, not Classical yakun, after in lam: Middle Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعَجُوزُ وَحَيٰوةِ شَبَابِكَ لَا بُدَّأَنِّي أُخَاطِرُ مَعَكَ بِرُوحِي وَأُبَلِّغُكَ مُرَادَكَ وَأُوصِلُكَ إِلَى مَا فِي خَاطِرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ʿajūzu wa-ḥayāti shabābika lā budda annī ukhāṭiru maʿaka bi-rūḥī wa-uballighuka murādaka wa-ūṣiluka ilā mā fī khāṭirika
sentences.l: And the old woman said to him: By the life of your youth, there is no escape (but) that I risk with you my soul, and make-you-reach your wish, and bring you to what (is) in your mind.
sentences.i: The old woman said to him, “By your young life, I will risk my own life with you, and get you what you want, and bring you to your heart's desire.”
sentences.n: wa-ḥayāti, “by the life of”: an oath, with wa- of swearing; the print spells ḥayāt with wāw (حيوة). lā budda annī, “it is inevitable that I”, which the print sets as لا بداني, joining budda to annī. khāṭara bi-, “to risk, to stake”: bi- marks the stake.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ كُلُّ مَا تَفْعَلِيهِ أُجَازِيكِ عَلَيْهِ وَتَلْتَقِيهِ فِي مِيزَانِكِ فَإِنَّكِ خَبِيرَةٌ بِالسِّيَاسَةِ وَعَارِفَةٌ بِأَبْوَابِ الدَّنَاسَةِ وَكُلُّ عَسِيرٍ عَلَيْكِ يَسِيرٌ وَاللَّهُ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā tāju al-mulūki kullu mā tafʿalīhi ujāzīki ʿalayhi wa-taltaqīhi fī mīzāniki fa-innaki khabīratun bi-al-siyāsati wa-ʿārifatun bi-abwābi al-danāsati wa-kullu ʿasīrin ʿalayki yasīrun wa-allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to her: All that you do, I will reward you for it, and you will meet it in your balance; for you (are) expert in the management and knowing in the doors of the filthiness, and every hard (thing) upon you (is) easy, and God (is) over every thing powerful.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to her, “Whatever you do, I will reward you for it, and you will find it weighed in your favour; for you are skilled in managing things and know every door to dirty dealing; nothing is hard for you, and God has power over all things.”
sentences.n: tafʿalīhi, “you do it”, without the -na of the Classical tafʿalīnahu: Middle Arabic. taltaqīhi, “you meet it”, for talqāhu; fī mīzāniki, “in your scale”, on the Day of Judgement, when deeds are weighed. al-danāsa, “filth, dirty dealing”: the praise is a backhanded one, and rhymes with al-siyāsa; so do ʿasīr / yasīr / qadīr. The print marks the feminine -ki with kasras here. khabīr bi-, ʿārif bi-, “skilled in, knowing of”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَ وَرَقَةً وَكَتَبَ فِيهَا هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadha waraqatan wa-kataba fīhā hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he took a paper and wrote in it these verses:
sentences.i: Then he took a sheet of paper and wrote these verses on it:
sentences.n: The print spells hādhihi with a final tāʾ marbūṭa (هذة).

sentences.t:
اَلَسْتَ تُهَدِّدُنِي بِالْقَتْلِ وَاعَجَبِي * وَالْقَتْلُ لِي رَاحَةٌ وَالْمَوْتُ مَقْدُورُ
وَالْمَوْتُ اَهْنَى لِصَبٍّ اَنْ تَطُولَ بِهِ * حَيوتُهُ وَهْوَ مَمْنُوعٌ وَمَقْهُورُ
بِاللّٰهِ زُورُوا مُحِبًّا قَلَّ نَاصِرُهُ * فَاِنَّنِي عَبْدُكُمْ وَالْعَبْدُ مَاسُورُ
يَاسَادَتِي فَارْحَمُونِي فِي مَحَبَّتِكُمْ * فَكُلُّ مَنْ يَعْشَقُ الْاَحْرَارَ مَعْذُورُ
sentences.tr:
a-lasta tuhaddidunī bi-al-qatli wā-ʿajabī * wa-al-qatlu lī rāḥatun wa-al-mawtu maqdūru
wa-al-mawtu ahnā li-ṣabbin an taṭūla bihi * ḥayātuhu wa-hwa mamnūʿun wa-maqhūru
bi-allāhi zūrū muḥibban qalla nāṣiruhu * fa-innanī ʿabdukum wa-al-ʿabdu māsūru
yā sādatī fa-rḥamūnī fī maḥabbatikum * fa-kullu man yaʿshaqu al-aḥrāra maʿdhūru
sentences.l:
Are you not threatening me with the killing — O my wonder! — * and the killing (is) for me a rest, and the death (is) decreed?
And the death (is) more wholesome for a lover than that his life be long with him * while he (is) forbidden and overpowered.
By God, visit a lover (whose) helper is few, * for indeed I (am) your slave, and the slave (is) captive.
O my masters, so have mercy on me in your love; * for every one who loves the free-born (is) excused.
sentences.i:
You threaten me with death — how strange! — * when death would be my rest, and death is fated anyway;
And death is sweeter for a lover than a long life * spent barred from what he loves, and overborne.
By God, come visit a lover with few to help him: * I am your slave, and a slave is a captive.
My masters, have pity on me in my love for you: * whoever loves the noble-born must be forgiven.
sentences.n: The print has واعربي, a misprint for wā-ʿajabī (واعجبي), “O my wonder!”, corrected here. Apart from this word the verse is given exactly as printed, with its vowels. wā- is the particle of lament or amazement. ahnā, “more wholesome”, is ahnaʾ without its hamza. ḥayātuhu is printed with wāw (حَيوتُهُ). wa-hwa is wa-huwa, shortened for the metre, as the print points it. māsūr is maʾsūr, “captive”, without its hamza. The beloved is addressed in the masculine, first in the singular (a-lasta, “are you not”) and then in the plural (zūrū, sādatī), as love poetry often does.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ تَنَفَّسَ الصُّعَدَاءَ وَبَكَى حَتَّى بَكَتِ الْعَجُوزُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu tanaffasa al-ṣuʿadāʾa wa-bakā ḥattā bakati al-ʿajūzu
sentences.l: Then he sighed the deep-sigh and wept, until the old woman wept.
sentences.i: Then he heaved a deep sigh and wept, until the old woman wept too.
sentences.n: tanaffasa al-ṣuʿadāʾ, “to breathe the upward breath”, to sigh deeply.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَخَذَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ مِنْهُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ طِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّ عَيْنًا فَلَا بُدَّأَنْ أُبَلِّغَكَ مَقْصُودَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika akhadhati al-waraqata minhu wa-qālat lahu ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan fa-lā budda an uballighaka maqṣūdaka
sentences.l: And after that she took the paper from him and said to him: Be good of soul and cool of eye, for there is no escape (but) that I make-you-reach your aim.
sentences.i: After that she took the paper from him and said, “Cheer up and be easy, for I will certainly get you what you are after.”
sentences.n: ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan, “be good of soul and cool of eye”: “take heart, be content”; a cool eye is a happy one. The print sets lā budda an as لا بدان, joining budda to an.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
